Reimagining Care
Beyond Mobility

This project follows prosthetic users of BMVSS (Jaipur Foot) back into daily life, where sweat, wounds, loose straps and makeshift repairs become problems with no one to ask. Grounded in field research, interviews and ecosystem mapping, it proposes an Aftercare Hygiene Kit and Saathi, a community support network, to carry care from the clinic into the home.

01
The problem

The device is fitted.
The care isn't.

After leaving the rehabilitation centre, users may face challenges with daily hygiene, prosthesis care, and accessing reliable guidance and ongoing support. That gap became the focus of this project.

500,000+amputees in India, with tens of thousands added every year
5%of amputees in India have access to prosthetic devices
10%of people needing assistive devices actually receive them
How might we make prosthetic aftercare more accessible, practical and continuous after users leave the rehabilitation centre?
Why it matters

Neglected post-prosthetic care can lead to:

InfectionsDiscomfortDevice rejectionReduced quality of life

It also reflects a gap in how healthcare is designed and delivered: dignity, continuity of care and user empowerment are often overlooked. The vision: reimagine prosthetic care beyond the point of delivery, with dignified, sustainable aftercare that empowers users in low-resource settings.

Goal

To explore how service design could make prosthetic aftercare more accessible, practical and continuous by connecting everyday care resources with ongoing community support.

Target users
  1. 1People with limb loss who use prosthetic devices and need ongoing aftercare.
  2. 2Caregivers and family members who support their daily recovery.
Key stakeholders

Prosthetists, rehabilitation professionals, healthcare providers and community organisations.

Research

What we researched before visiting BMVSS

This was collective secondary research done by the whole class before the field visit to BMVSS Jaipur. Our shared FigJam board, “Designing Dignity: Secondary Research”, was organised into five pages, one for each topic we covered. Step through them.

These five topics were the groundwork the class took into the field visit to BMVSS Jaipur.

Secondary research

What the literature doesn’t cover

Reviewed studies treat prosthetic care through access, rehabilitation and clinical evaluation: device distribution, mobility outcomes, institutional systems. India-focused work flags centralised delivery, too few trained professionals and limited rural reach. Global work stresses holistic care and follow-up.

Yet one gap is consistent across the papers: how people maintain, manage and adapt to prostheses in daily life, especially hygiene, affordability and awareness.

Bars are a qualitative reading of the essay’s literature summary, not a paper count.

03

Into the field

The team combined secondary research with qualitative field interviews with prosthetic users and other stakeholders, then brought interviews together to compare experiences and find recurring gaps.

Primary research · the interview guide

Questions with everyday texture

Semi-structured interviews with prosthetic users and caregivers, chosen because they had recently been fitted and were navigating post-discharge care. The guide moves from background to belonging, and its probes are tuned to Indian daily life: sitting cross-legged, sitting on the floor, festivals.

7–13 April 2026 · BMVSS Jaipur

Voices from the field

Over seven days the team conducted 100+ interviews with prosthetic users, caregivers, family members and BMVSS staff. Six insights stood out for aftercare. Quotes are verbatim from the team’s transcripts, shown with English translations. Open a card to see the field notes behind it.

From staff interviews

Names are shared with participants’ consent. Quotes in Hindi are as recorded in the team’s transcripts; English translations are added for readers.

Synthesis · ten insights

Connecting the dots

I synthesised the interviews into ten insights. Each card separates what was heard and seen in the field from my reading of it. Three insights shaped the aftercare focus; the rest are real problems I set aside.

04

Personas

Ramesh is working towards independence and a return to everyday life. Savitri is the caregiver who supports daily care and decision-making. Aftercare affects not only the person using the prosthesis, but the people supporting them. Both personas lack clarity between normal discomfort and a serious problem, which delays action, and both lean on neighbours and temporary fixes because structured guidance is out of reach.

Aftercare guidance has to reach users and caregivers.

System · ecosystem map

Many actors. Weakly connected.

Direct interactionIndirect or weak

Select an actor. Solid lines are direct interactions; dotted lines are indirect or weak.

Caregivers, local technicians and neighbours form the most active support. Doctors and institutions engage only episodically, particularly after discharge. Government schemes and NGOs support but lack continuous involvement. Most interactions turn inconsistent, or drop off, after the initial fitting.

Delayed medical attentionReliance on informal adviceImproper use & maintenance
System · touchpoint map

Fourteen stages, one loop

I mapped the patient journey across fourteen stages, from injury to long-term use. Six stages lead up to the centre. From Accessing the service onwards the journey becomes a cycle: treatment, life with the prosthetic, problems at home, and a crisis that sends people back to headquarters to start again. Narrowing the scope

Two stages, studied in depth

With limited time, I couldn’t go deep on all fourteen stages. Stages 10 and 11, Return home & reality and Problem emergence, held the most unresolved challenges: support is dense at the centre, but after discharge structure falls away. Users get less clear guidance and less access to professional help, and have to manage more on their own. I narrowed my research to these two stages and analysed their pain points in detail.

Reflection · how my thinking changed

The challenge is not access, but continuity of care.
Initial briefDesign a decentralised support system that strengthens trust in local prosthetic service networks while letting users safely maintain and manage devices beyond the Jaipur Foot centre.
Final briefDesign a simple, practical aftercare solution that empowers prosthetic users and their caregivers to manage hygiene, discomfort and device maintenance with confidence and clarity.
What shifted (my reading)From rebuilding trust in a local service network to equipping users and caregivers directly, then reconnecting them to that network through Saathi.

Service blueprint · the chosen stage

From discharge to long-term aftercare

This blueprint shows the key touchpoints, user actions, and supporting processes from discharge to long-term aftercare, highlighting how the proposed solution integrates into the user journey.

User touchpointsSupporting processes
Ground levelUser actions and experiences
  • Patient receives prosthesis, hygiene kit, and initial instructions.
  • Introduced to Saathi (peer support group).
  • Given contact details.
  • User starts using prosthesis at home.
  • Follows hygiene and maintenance guidance.
  • Faces real-life challenges (e.g. discomfort, sweating).
  • User reaches out to Saathi for guidance or support.
  • Interacts with local peer group (calls / WhatsApp / meetups).
  • Seeks help for maintenance or concerns.
  • User shares feedback on challenges, kit usefulness, and support received.
  • Reports issues or needs additional guidance.
  • User experience and feedback help improve the service over time.
  • Better support, resources, and processes are developed based on real user needs.
Line of visibility
Backend levelSupporting processes and system enablers
  • Kit is assembled and packed.
  • Visual materials provided (booklet/card).
  • Patient and caregiver briefed on usage.
  • Contact details shared for support.
  • Guidance provided for common issues.
  • Remote support made available (phone/WhatsApp).
  • Escalation path for serious concerns.
  • Community coordinator/mentor assigns user to local group.
  • Mentors and support network respond to queries.
  • Basic troubleshooting guidance provided.
  • Feedback collected through calls, WhatsApp or in-person methods.
  • Common issues documented.
  • Insights shared with team for service improvement.
  • Feedback analysed periodically.
  • Kit content and support processes updated.
  • Service improvements implemented.

09

What I couldn’t test yet

Time was the main constraint. The concept is grounded in research but has not yet been validated with the people it is designed for.

01Hygiene Kit not user-tested

The kit, its contents and the illustrated guide were not tested with prosthetic users, caregivers or clinicians.

02Saathi not piloted

Peer groups, coordinator onboarding, consent-based contact sharing and support channels remain untested in a real community.

03System is a proposal

The service blueprint and five-step framework, including the policy route through DEPwD, are proposals still to be validated.

04Two stages, not fourteen

Time limited the deep dive to two aftercare stages, so pain points elsewhere in the journey were not analysed in depth.

10

Reflection

My contribution

The secondary research was a class-wide group activity before the field visit. At BMVSS, every member of the team conducted interviews: over 100 in total, with prosthetic users, caregivers, family members and BMVSS staff. We then combined them to form shared insights.

Everything after that was my own work: narrowing the scope, the journey mapping and two-stage deep dive, the pain-point analysis, ideation, the Aftercare Hygiene Kit, the Saathi system and the service blueprint.

What I would do differently
  • Prototype earlier. Put a rough kit and guide in front of users and caregivers before refining the details.
  • Plan time for validation from the start, so testing isn’t squeezed out at the end.
  • Co-design with prosthetists sooner, to check what is clinically safe to recommend at home.
  • Follow people home. Speak with users after discharge, not only when they return to the centre.
